description: On a mission to expedite lunar exploration
summary:
Earth Bound is an interactive web map that locates regions on Earth that closely resemble Mars and the Moon in terms of not only visuals, but atmospheric conditions, terrain, and more. Space agencies test rovers, habitats and instruments at “analog” sites, but picking and comparing them is slow and mostly manual.

We built a single-page tool that scores locations against five lunar and Martian targets (Mars-Meridiani, Mars-Jezero, Moon-Mare, Moon-SouthPole and Moon-LavaTubePit). It compares Earth conditions (temperature, day–night swing, aridity, solar, wind, dust) with target values, using NASA POWER climate data fetched live, plus NASA Mars/Moon Trek imagery and elevation for context. Users switch between flat map and globe, toggle Mars or Moon, adjust factor weights, and click any of 12 curated analog sites, from Qatar’s Khor Al Adaid to Antarctica’s Dry Valleys. Each site opens an explanatory summary with match scores, expedition uses, data confidence and limits.

It matters because it makes analog selection transparent, comparable and easy to explore, helping teams prepare for exploration on Earth first. As well as the local aspect, and making it accessible for children.
details: Earth Bound is an interactive browser app that finds the places on Earth that most closely resemble the surface of Mars and the Moon, so that rovers, habitats and instruments can be tested on Earth before they fly. Space agencies already use “analog” sites for this, but choosing and comparing them usually means scattered literature and expert judgement. Our tool puts that comparison in one transparent, explorable view. The user picks Mars or the Moon, and the app compares Earth conditions (temperature, day–night swing, aridity, solar, wind and dust) with the reference values for the chosen target. Each factor is turned into a similarity of 100% at an exact match, falling linearly to 0% once the gap reaches a set range, and the factors are combined into an overall score. The result appears as a colour heat map that users can view on a flat map or a globe, with factors that can be switched on and off and re-weighted. Twelve curated analog sites are pinned on the map, from Qatar’s Khor Al Adaid and Iran’s Dasht-e Lut to Chile’s Atacama, Antarctica’s Dry Valleys and Canada’s Haughton Crater. Hovering a pin enlarges it and shows a short tooltip, and clicking opens a full summary. The summary includes a per-factor match table (Earth value, target value, difference, range and match %), the site’s match against all five targets (Mars-Meridiani, Mars-Jezero, Moon-Mare, Moon-SouthPole and Moon-LavaTubePit), what expeditions the site is good for, a confidence rating for each value, the sources behind the Earth values, and a plain statement of the limits of the analogy. A 3D terrain view and NASA Mars or Moon imagery and elevation sit alongside, so the user can compare the Earth site with its target visually. The project uses NASA POWER climatology, fetched live for temperature, precipitation, humidity, sunlight, wind and aerosol data, and NASA Solar System Treks layers (Viking MDIM, MGS MOLA, LRO WAC and LRO LOLA) for context. It also uses Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery and open terrain tiles for the base map and 3D views. It is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using D3.js for maps and projections, TopoJSON for borders and three.js for the 3D terrain. A Python script assembles everything into a single self-contained HTML file from an Excel workbook that holds the sites, targets and scoring formula, so the model can be updated by editing the spreadsheet and rebuilding. It is hosted free on GitHub Pages, so anyone can open it with no install or server. We were careful about honesty and uncertainty. Some site values are estimates, and terrain roughness is still an index rather than a value computed from an elevation model. The app labels estimates and confidence levels and states that Earth cannot reproduce lunar or Martian gravity, vacuum, atmosphere or radiation. Values between named sites are interpolated, so the heat map shows trends rather than measurements. We hope the project helps students, mission planners and the public see where Earth can stand in for other worlds. A natural next step is to replace the remaining estimates with values computed from NASA and Copernicus elevation data.
